title: Remove Duplicate Letters
statement:
You get a string `s` of lowercase letters. Delete characters from `s` (keeping the rest in their original order) until each distinct letter of `s` is left exactly once: no letter may be lost entirely and none may remain twice.

Many such strings can usually be formed. Return the one that comes first in alphabetical (lexicographic) order.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

The answer keeps one copy of every letter, so the only freedom is *which* copy. Reading `s` left to right, we want small letters as early as possible. When a new letter `ch` arrives and the last kept letter is bigger, that bigger letter would be better placed later, but we may only drop it if another copy of it still appears further on. Keeping the chosen letters on a stack that we pop under exactly that condition gives a monotonic stack. (A slower greedy tries each candidate letter for each output position and checks the rest of the string, about O(26² · n).)

## Approach

1. Record `last`, the final index of each letter in `s`.
2. Walk `s` with index `i` and current letter `ch`.
3. If `ch` is already on the stack (`inStack`), skip it: its earlier copy is already in a good place.
4. While the top of `stack` is larger than `ch` and that top letter occurs again after `i`, pop it and remove it from `inStack`.
5. Push `ch` and mark it in `inStack`.
6. Join the stack into the answer.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "bcabc"`, so `last` is b → 3, c → 4, a → 2. `i = 0` pushes `b`; `i = 1` pushes `c` (stack `bc`). At `i = 2`, `a` is smaller than `c`, and `c` returns at 4, so pop it; `b` returns at 3, so pop it too; push `a`. Then `b` and `c` are pushed, and the stack `abc` is the answer.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): every letter is pushed and popped at most once.
- Space: O(1) extra beyond the output: the stack, `last` and `inStack` hold at most 26 letters.

## Pitfalls

- Skipping a letter already on the stack is essential: without it, `"abacb"` would pop `b` for the second `a` and end up as `"aacb"`, with `a` twice.
- Pop only when the top letter appears again later (`last > i`); otherwise that letter would vanish.
- The result must be a subsequence of `s`, so simply sorting the distinct letters is wrong (`"cbacdcbc"` gives `"acdb"`, not `"abcd"`).

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `last` | final index of each letter in `s` |
| `stack` | letters chosen so far, in output order |
| `inStack` | letters currently on the stack |
| `i`, `ch` | current index and letter |

narration.2: last will map every letter to the final index where it appears.
narration.4: Later indices overwrite earlier ones, so the final index wins.
narration.6: The stack holds the answer built so far, one copy per letter.
narration.7: inStack lets us check in constant time whether a letter is already used.
narration.9: Read the string from left to right.
narration.11: This letter is already placed; a later copy cannot improve the answer.
narration.14: The top letter is bigger than ch and comes back later, so it is better placed after ch.
narration.15: Pop it and forget that it was used; a later copy will add it again.
narration.17: Place ch on top of the stack.
narration.20: The stack, read bottom to top, is the smallest valid string.
